borders.before: lecturer introduction, course outline, and intended learning outcomes
borders.after: definition of cancer as a genetic and microenvironmental disease evolving on a cellular scale
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is opening framing that sets expectations and learning outcomes, while subtopic 2 begins substantive scientific exposition on what cancer is.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no alternative boundary since subtopic 1 is purely introductory and subtopic 2 immediately begins the core lecture material.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would mix preliminary course administration and framing with substantive pathological concepts.

borders.before: epidemiological evidence showing worldwide and migrant variations in cancer incidence
borders.after: mechanisms of infectious pathogens (such as H. pylori, HPV, EBV, and Aspergillus) in carcinogenesis
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 6 concludes the broad overview of environmental versus genetic contributions to cancer incidence, whereas subtopic 7 begins a detailed, mechanistic examination of specific carcinogenic agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 6 would prematurely group broad geographic epidemiology with specific biochemical pathways; moving it to subtopic 8 would separate the general overview of pathogens from the specific Burkitt lymphoma case study.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would conflate high-level population risk and public understanding with detailed molecular and cellular mechanisms of individual carcinogens.

borders.before: tissue-specific metabolic activation of chemical carcinogens such as aromatic amines in the bladder
borders.after: asbestos, chronic inflammation, and the mechanistic distinction between tumor initiators and promoters
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopics 7–13 focus on agents that induce direct or metabolically generated DNA damage, whereas subtopic 14 shifts to non-mutagenic agents, chronic inflammation, and the initiator–promoter paradigm.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 15 would leave asbestos separated from the two-stage Berenbaum model of promotion it illustrates; moving it to subtopic 13 would place chemical mutagens with promoter concepts.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would blur the fundamental distinction between direct DNA-damaging mutagens and non-mutagenic tumor promoters.

borders.before: a summary of direct and indirect mutagens, promoters, metabolic activation, and developmental susceptibility windows
borders.after: using high-throughput whole-genome sequencing to identify distinct mutational signatures of carcinogens
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 provides a summary of biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis, while subtopic 18 starts a new section on experimental and analytical methodologies used to prove and detect carcinogenicity.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 17 would incorrectly place the summary of mechanisms into the methodology topic; moving it to subtopic 19 would separate genomic sequencing approaches from the other testing methodologies.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would merge the biological principles of carcinogenesis with the experimental methods used by scientists to detect and prove carcinogenicity.

borders.before: in vitro testing using the Ames Salmonella reversion assay and its biological limitations
borders.after: lecture wrap-up, practical risk-versus-benefit considerations of carcinogen exposure, and final conclusions
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 21 concludes the review of scientific assay systems, whereas subtopic 22 serves as the closing framing summarizing the lecture and discussing risk-benefit trade-offs.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no other logical split, as subtopic 21 is clearly focused on experimental toxicology and subtopic 22 is the concluding wrap-up.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would merge formal closing remarks with the technical evaluation of bacterial mutagenesis assays.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2–3 establish theoretical concepts of cancer evolution, endogenous mutational burden, and genetic predispositions, whereas subtopics 4–6 focus on everyday environmental exposures, public perception debates, and global epidemiological variations.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 through 6 collectively address the overarching conceptual question of whether cancer is driven by intrinsic bad luck or environmental factors, combining biological principles with epidemiological evidence.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 7–8 deal specifically with biological pathogens and viral oncogenesis (notably Burkitt lymphoma), while subtopics 9–13 detail dietary, physical, and chemical mutagens requiring metabolic activation and adduct formation.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 7 to 13 function as a single comprehensive catalogue of specific exogenous mutagens and their molecular mechanisms of inducing DNA alterations.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14–15 focus on tumor promotion via chronic inflammation and PKC signaling pathways, while subtopics 16–17 explore host developmental timing, age at exposure, and tissue susceptibility windows.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: All four subtopics (14–17) deal with non-mutational and contextual determinants of cancer risk—including microenvironmental promotion, inflammatory priming, and host tissue life stages.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 18 focuses on modern bioinformatic mutational signatures from DNA sequencing, whereas subtopics 19–21 review traditional epidemiological biobanks, in vivo animal bioassays, and in vitro bacterial testing.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 through 21 are united by the single investigative question of how researchers prove and quantify carcinogenicity across molecular, population, animal, and in vitro levels.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer introduces herself, the cancer lecture series, and the key learning outcomes regarding environmental carcinogens and cancer biology.

topics.label: Origins, Drivers, and Epidemiological Evidence of Cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore cancer as an evolutionary genetic process driven by a balance of endogenous metabolic errors, genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and global epidemiological patterns.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Pathogen, Chemical, and Physical Carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail how specific biological pathogens, dietary toxins, radiation, and chemical carcinogens undergo metabolic processing and induce DNA adducts and mutations.

topics.label: Tumor Initiation, Promotion, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain the distinction between mutational tumor initiators and inflammatory promoters, alongside the role of host tissue development and life-stage susceptibility in carcinogenesis.

topics.label: Methodologies for Assessing and Proving Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics review the analytical techniques used to determine carcinogenicity, including mutational signature sequencing, epidemiological biobanks, animal toxicology bioassays, and in vitro Ames tests.

topics.label: Summary and Risk-Benefit Analysis
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer summarizes the main principles of environmental carcinogenesis and concludes with the everyday risk-benefit trade-offs associated with carcinogenic exposures.
